questions.question: Q1. The reference build (fpv5 chassis, 5" tri-blade props, 1806 motors, 4S/1500 pack, no payload) has an all-up mass of about 529 g. What level-flight thrust must the motors produce?

explanations.a: Incorrect — that is roughly half the required thrust.
explanations.b: Correct — T = m·g = 0.529 kg × 9.807 m/s² ≈ 5.19 N.
explanations.c: Incorrect — that is double the required thrust.
explanations.d: Incorrect — that overstates mass by a factor of 10 (as if mass were 5.29 kg).

questions.question: Q2. Four 5" (0.127 m diameter) propellers give a total disk area A_disk = 4·π·(0.0635)² ≈ 0.0507 m². With T ≈ 5.19 N and ρ = 1.225 kg/m³, what is the hover-induced velocity v_h = √(T / (2ρA_disk))?

explanations.b: Incorrect — that is roughly half the correct value.
explanations.d: Incorrect — that is roughly double the correct value.

questions.question: Q3. Using P_ind(0) = T·v_h with T ≈ 5.19 N and v_h ≈ 6.47 m/s, what is the reference build's ideal hover power?

explanations.b: Incorrect — that is roughly half the correct value.
explanations.c: Correct — P_ind(0) = 5.19 × 6.47 ≈ 33.5 W, the momentum-theory hover power floor.
explanations.d: Incorrect — that is roughly double the correct value.

questions.question: Q4. For the reference build, sweeping the cruise-power curve from 2-20 m/s gives a minimum near which airspeed, and roughly what power?

explanations.a: Incorrect — 2 m/s is close to hover, where power is still near its high induced-power floor, not the minimum.
explanations.b: Correct — the theory worked example shows the minimum near V ≈ 9.5 m/s at about 26 W, the maximum-endurance operating point.
explanations.c: Incorrect — at 15 m/s parasitic power has already pushed cruise power well above the minimum.
explanations.d: Incorrect — 20 m/s is near the top of the sweep, where parasitic power dominates and cruise power is well above the minimum.

questions.question: Q5. For the same reference build, the maximum-range speed (minimising power per unit distance) is found near V ≈ 13.5 m/s. Compared with the maximum-endurance speed of ≈ 9.5 m/s, what does this confirm?

answers.a: The two speeds are identical for this build
answers.b: Maximum-range speed is always slower than maximum-endurance speed
answers.c: Maximum-range speed is faster than maximum-endurance speed, as the theory predicts
answers.d: Airspeed has no effect on which optimum applies

explanations.a: Incorrect — 13.5 m/s and 9.5 m/s are clearly different speeds.
explanations.b: Incorrect — this reverses the correct relationship; range speed is the faster one.
explanations.c: Correct — the max-range speed sits to the right of the power-curve minimum, confirming it is always faster than the max-endurance speed.
explanations.d: Incorrect — airspeed is exactly the variable that distinguishes the two optimum operating points.

questions.question: Q6. In the virtual lab simulation's Mission Energy sub-experiment, a 4S/1500 mAh pack has a rated energy E_batt = 14.8 V × 1.5 Ah ≈ 22.2 Wh. A 500 m out-and-back mission at V = 10 m/s (30/60/30 s hover phases) costs the reference build about 1.85 Wh. What does this confirm about the mission?

answers.a: The mission fails — the pack cannot supply enough energy
answers.b: The mission passes with a very large energy margin, since 1.85 Wh is a small fraction of the 22.2 Wh pack
answers.c: The mission exactly exhausts the pack
answers.d: The pack capacity is irrelevant to whether the mission passes

explanations.a: Incorrect — 1.85 Wh is far below the 22.2 Wh rated energy; the mission does not fail here.
explanations.b: Correct — even after the ≈0.55 electrical-to-aerodynamic efficiency factor, 1.85 Wh is a small slice of a 22.2 Wh pack, so the mission passes with substantial margin to spare.
explanations.c: Incorrect — 1.85 Wh is nowhere near the pack's full rated energy.
explanations.d: Incorrect — the PASS/FAIL verdict is defined precisely by comparing mission energy against usable pack capacity.

questions.question: Q7. In the Range-Payload sub-experiment, on the 4S/1500 pack cruising at 10 m/s, doubling payload from 200 g to 400 g cuts range from about 9.5 km to about 6.2 km. What percentage reduction in range does this represent, and why is it so large for only a doubling of payload?

answers.a: About 10% — because payload barely affects range
answers.b: About 35% — because induced power grows super-linearly with weight (T^1.5 at hover, even steeper in forward flight), so the extra mass costs disproportionately more power
answers.c: About 65% — because range is inversely proportional to the square of payload
answers.d: About 100% — because doubling payload always halves range exactly, plus a fixed penalty

explanations.a: Incorrect — 10% understates the actual drop shown by the worked example.
explanations.b: Correct — (9.5 - 6.2)/9.5 ≈ 0.35, a roughly one-third cut, driven by induced power's super-linear scaling with the heavier build's weight.
explanations.c: Incorrect — the model does not use an inverse-square relationship between range and payload.
explanations.d: Incorrect — the actual reduction (about a third) is considerably less than a full halving, let alone 100%.

questions.question: Q8. During the Range-Payload sub-experiment, the simulator sweeps the same payload range across three reference packs — 3S/2200 mAh, 4S/1500 mAh and 6S/5000 mAh — while leaving the rest of the build's mass exactly as configured in Input Parameters. What does this simulator behaviour mean for reading the resulting envelope?

answers.a: Each curve already includes the extra physical weight of its own pack, so the comparison is a true apples-to-apples flight-weight trade-off
answers.b: The three curves differ only because of each pack's usable Watt-hours — the simulator does not add the heavier real-world mass of a bigger pack, so the envelope isolates the energy-capacity effect alone
answers.c: The battery choice has no effect at all on the plotted curves
answers.d: The simulator recomputes the airframe's centre of gravity for each pack before sweeping

explanations.a: Incorrect — the dry mass used for every curve stays fixed at the currently selected battery's mass; a real 6S/5000 pack would be heavier than a 4S/1500 one, and that difference is not modelled here.
explanations.b: Correct — rangeFor() only varies with each reference pack's rated Wh in this sweep; total mass is not re-derived per pack, so the three curves show the pure effect of energy capacity on range.
explanations.c: Incorrect — battery choice clearly shifts each curve, through its usable energy term.
explanations.d: Incorrect — the simulator has no centre-of-gravity model; this experiment only tracks total mass, drag and power.

questions.question: Q9. In the virtual lab simulation, if you lengthen the cruise-out and cruise-back legs in the Mission Energy sub-experiment's phase-duration editor while keeping payload and battery fixed, what happens to the PASS/FAIL verdict?

answers.a: Nothing changes — phase durations don't affect the verdict
answers.b: The verdict always stays PASS regardless of duration
answers.c: Total mission energy rises with the added cruise time, shrinking the margin against usable pack energy and eventually flipping the verdict to FAIL
answers.d: Longer cruise legs reduce the mission energy because cruise power is lower than hover power

explanations.a: Incorrect — the phase durations are exactly what the energy summation is built from; changing them changes the total directly.
explanations.b: Incorrect — energy grows without bound as duration grows, so a long enough leg will always exceed the pack's usable energy.
explanations.c: Correct — E_total sums power times duration over every phase; stretching the cruise legs adds proportionally more Watt-hours until the usable pack energy is exceeded and the verdict flips.
explanations.d: Incorrect — whether cruise power is lower than hover power depends on the chosen airspeed, and even when it is, more time still means more energy, not less.

questions.question: Q10. In the virtual lab simulation, moving the Density Altitude slider upward (increasing altitude) before running Power Profiling changes air density ρ. What happens to the U-shaped cruise-power curve as a result?

answers.a: The curve is unaffected — altitude only matters for the Range-Payload sub-experiment
answers.b: Both the parasitic-power term and the hover-induced-velocity term change, because both F_D(V) and v_h depend on ρ, so the whole curve — and its minimum — shifts
answers.c: Only the parasitic drag term changes; induced power is independent of air density
answers.d: The curve becomes flat because thinner air removes all drag

explanations.a: Incorrect — altitude changes ρ, which every metric in this experiment depends on through drag and induced velocity.
explanations.b: Correct — F_D(V) = ½ρV²C_dA falls with lower ρ, and v_h = √(T/(2ρA_disk)) rises with lower ρ, so thinner air at altitude reshapes both halves of the curve and moves its minimum.
explanations.c: Incorrect — v_h, and hence induced power, explicitly depends on ρ through the same formula used since Section 2.
explanations.d: Incorrect — thinner air reduces drag but does not eliminate it, and induced power actually rises as density falls.
